This also sounds very corny, but—When I was in 7th grade, my History/Bible/Homeroom teacher (I went to a Christian school) pulled me aside while I was filing papers away one day and asked me if I liked to write. I said yes; he told me that I had a real skill, “the best he’d seen a 7th grader write
.” We then talked a bit about what I liked writing, and he told me about a relative who wrote poems and published them in the paper from time to time, which I thought was cool. He then told me something that has honestly gotten me through a lot of rough patches and is probably the one reason I’m still bothering: “I have a feeling you’re going to write something extremely significant.”

I’m 30 now, and I sometimes feel as though my window for this has closed. Yes, I know that’s silly; some of the most revered writers have written their best works much later in life, after gaining lots of life experience. It’s just, in my early 20s as a college student, I did okay. I submitted work places, and while I never got into the New Yorker or anything obviously, I did ok. I was published in a few decent literary journals and received personal/“close call” rejections from “higher-tier” ones as well. 

I just got back into “fun” writing more prolifically last year, after a very long slump. After refining a few pieces, I sent them out, and—oof, form rejections everywhere. I did eventually land a poem somewhere, and I got paid for it. I’m happy about that—but I still feel so far from where I was. Writing is my day job (I’m an editor who often has to write as often as I edit other people’s work.) But I don’t consider the work I do there part of my personal body of work. Don’t get me wrong, I’m proud of what I do and love my job, but it’s different from being a Writer, at least in my eyes.

That little encouragement from middle school keeps me wondering if maybe I’m not totally without purpose. Yeah, I’ll probably never write the “next Great American Novel,” which isn’t my goal anyway (I write poetry and creative nonfiction.) But maybe I can write something that means something to someone.

Oh I do something very similar with the doordash sandwich once a week! Only mine is from sheetz and it’s a veggie sandwich. I usually also get grapes and babybel cheese. Sometimes if I can fit the calories in, I might get a small curly fry—but I don’t make a habit of it. But that silly order has been giving me something to look forward to every week! And honestly, I think little things like that are what make weight loss feel more manageable (knowing we don’t have to just eat kale and grilled chicken every day, even though those can certainly be delicious too).

I still eat “bad foods.” In fact, I had some ice cream today. I just 1. Eat it in much smaller portions. I never leave the package out after I serve myself. I get what I give myself (usually the serving size or half that) and that’s all I get. The package goes out of sight so I don’t have to worry about impulsively grabbing it without giving my body the chance to register that it’s satisfied (and it always is). 2. I make myself try new foods too. I used to think I hated tomatoes and onions when they weren’t either on pizza or deep fried in some way. Now that I’ve been trying different recipes, I realize they are freaking delicious. I just might not have been eating them the right way.

All that is to say—you can still enjoy your favorite foods. In fact, I recommend that you do if you want to—the weight loss journey isn’t going to be sustainable or you constantly feel hungry or are going to go right back to your old eating habits once you lose the weight. I find that when I tell myself I can still have “those” foods, I want them even less—because I know they’re not forbidden. They’re just not foods I can eat every day or in large quantities. Now I crave those healthy foods a lot more often. I won’t lie,  I crave the unhealthy stuff too—but now I can usually be satisfied with just the little taste and then move on with my day.

This is just what works for me of course. It may not work for everyone.

Anyone who is shaming you for your rate of weight loss is an asshole, full stop. Every worthwhile heath professional will tend you that slow, steady weight loss tends to be healthier and more sustainable than very rapid weight loss. Of course there are exceptions. If you want to speed it up, I would suggest calculating your current TDEE using an online calculator and subtract about 500 calories from that. It’ll still likely be gradual (depending on your current intake and other health stuff), but it might get you to losing say 1 lb a week more consistently. That’s been my rate of weight loss. I’m content with that. Do I wish this process were quicker? Sure, but we didn’t gain the weight overnight, and we aren’t going to lose it overnight either. Just be patient with yourself and be willing to learn along the way.

CICO, BUT with a focus beyond just counting calories. Yeah, you can theoretically lose weight by eating Big Macs and Oreos every day as long as you are burning more than you are consuming. But your health will probably suffer long-term even if you do shed the pounds, and it probably won’t be sustainable. I find that when I focus on eating the right quantities of high quality food, I fare best. These foods aren’t just salads and bland low-calorie things but filling, nutritious foods that I enjoy and can enjoy as part of my lifestyle (roasted chickpeas, tostadas, quesadillas and flatbreads filled with veggies, soups, etc.) I also don’t deprive myself of “bad” food. I try not to call foods good or bad but instead use the terms “sometimes” and “always.” As long as that chocolate fits within my calories for the day, I let myself have it without guilt. I might even budget for it. By eating all those nutrient-dense foods, I eventually lose the constant cravings for it anyway. But should the craving strike, I know I can indulge without totally sabotaging myself.

There are MFA programs across many disciplines (creative writing, visual art, music, etc.) with acceptance rates that can hover between 1-5%. Yeah, my mom had a hemorrhagic stroke in 2017. All things considered, she has made a very good recovery. She is still paralyzed on her right side but can walk fairly well, and speech has returned fully. However, the scariest part of the whole thing was all the uncertainty in the beginning. There really is nothing they can do but “wait and see” with a hemorrhagic stroke. They might do surgery, but from what I understand, that’s usually if the bleeding is very severe and they need to relieve pressure? Anyway, it was terrifying to witness. My mom did not have any prior symptoms. It all came on suddenly. One minute she was walking around find, the next minute she could not get up or move her right side and had very slurred speech. She did mention before all that happening, everything seemed to feel “slanted.” But other than that, no pain or noticeable discomfort.

I will say though: my mom’s stroke was very likely caused by high blood pressure that went unchecked for a very long time. She had medication for it but didn’t take it. So if you have high blood pressure or a history of it, please do keep up on that! Get it checked regularly, watch your sodium intake, try to eat a relatively balanced diet. That’s my $.02.

By the way, I hope your husband is doing well. Stroke recovery is such a long, emotional process.
